question: M is mother of siblings N and O. P is the child of O. M's brother has a son, who in turn has a child Q. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the precise relation between P and Q?
explanation: O and N are siblings; O's child P is N's niece/nephew. M's brother’s son is a first cousin to N and O; his child Q is that cousin’s child, i.e., N’s first cousin once removed. P (child of O) and Q (child of N’s cousin) share the same great‑grandparents (M’s parents), making them second cousins. No other term is more exact.
choices: C) C) First cousins once removed

question: John is the son of Mary. Mary’s brother is Peter. Peter’s daughter is Lisa. Lisa’s son is Tom. What is Tom’s relation to John using standard English kinship terms?
explanation: John’s mother’s brother is his maternal uncle; the uncle’s daughter is John’s first cousin, and her son is one generation down, making him John’s first cousin once removed.

question: M and N are siblings. M is married to X and N is married to Y. X and Y are also siblings. Their respective children, A (child of M & X) and B (child of N & Y), have no other familial connections. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation between A and B?
explanation: A and B share both sets of grandparents (the parents of M/N and the parents of X/Y). This makes them first cousins, but with the double sharing of ancestry, the exact term is "double first cousins".

question: Let P be a person. Let G be P’s father’s mother (paternal grandmother). Let S be G’s sister. Let X be the child of S, and let M be the child of X. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy, remarriage allowed), what is the precise relation between M and P?
explanation: G and S are sisters, so their children F (P’s father) and X are first cousins. The children of first cousins—P and M—are second cousins. Hence the exact term is “second cousins.”

question: John and Mary share the same mother but have different fathers (they are half‑siblings). John’s daughter Lily and Mary’s son Peter each have one child: Lily’s child Emma and Peter’s child Noah. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy), what is the most precise relationship between Emma and Noah?
explanation: Lily and Peter are half‑first cousins, sharing only one grandparent. Their children therefore share only one pair of great‑grandparents, making Emma and Noah half‑second cousins—the exact term for this level of shared ancestry.

question: John and Mary are married. Mary has a brother Tom, who is married to Lisa. Lisa’s father is also John’s father (John and Lisa are half‑brothers sharing the same father). Who is Tom to John’s daughter Emma?
explanation: John and Lisa share a father, so Lisa is John’s half‑sister. Tom, being Lisa’s husband, is Emma’s half‑uncle by marriage. No standard term exists for a half‑uncle‑in‑law, so the relation is not uniquely named in standard English kinship.

question: L has exactly one sibling, a sister named M. N has exactly one sibling, a brother named O. M and O are married and have a child P. L also has a child Q. Assuming no other intermarriages, what is the precise kinship term for P in relation to Q?
explanation: M is L’s sister, so P is the child of L’s sibling, making P a niece/nephew of L. Q is L’s child, so Q is the child of L’s sibling’s sibling. Thus P and Q share the same set of grandparents (the parents of L and M), which defines them as first cousins.

question: Two brothers, John and Mike, each marry a sister, Anna and Beth respectively (John‑Anna are the elder siblings, Mike‑Beth the younger). John and Anna have a son Carl; Mike and Beth have a daughter Dana. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation between Carl and Dana?
explanation: Carl and Dana are children of two brothers and two sisters who married each other. They share both sets of grandparents, so their relationship is more specific than ordinary first cousins: they are double first cousins.

question: Person X has a mother whose only brother (M) has a daughter Y, and a father whose only sister (S) has a son Z. Y and Z marry and have a child W. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is the precise relationship of W to X?
explanation: Y is X's maternal first cousin; Z is X's paternal first cousin. A child of a first cousin is a first cousin once removed. W is the child of two first cousins of X, but each lineage gives the same term, so W is X's first cousin once removed.
choices: B) B) First cousin once removed

question: A is the son of the brother of B’s mother. B is the daughter of the sister of A’s father. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is the precise relation of A to B?
explanation: A is the child of B’s maternal uncle, making him B’s maternal first cousin. Simultaneously, B is the child of A’s paternal aunt, making her A’s paternal first cousin. Sharing both sets of grandparents, they are double first cousins—the most specific term.

question: John’s mother has only one brother, Peter, and John’s father has only one sister, Mary. Peter’s only child is Sarah, and Mary’s only child is also Sarah. Using standard English kinship terms, what is Sarah’s precise relation to John?
explanation: Peter is John’s maternal uncle; Mary is John’s paternal aunt. Both have the same child Sarah. Thus Sarah is the child of John’s uncle on one side and aunt on the other, sharing both of John’s grandparent pairs. That is the definition of a double first cousin, the most precise term.

question: M is married to W. W’s brother B is married to M’s sister S. B and S have a child C. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy, remarriage allowed), what is C’s precise relation to M?
explanation: S is M’s sister, so C is M’s niece/nephew by blood. B is M’s brother‑in‑law, but that does not create a separate term; the blood link via S determines the relation uniquely as niece/nephew.

question: John’s parents are Mary and Peter. Mary’s brother Tom is married to Lisa. Lisa’s sister Nina is married to Carl, who is Peter’s brother. Emma is the child of Tom and Lisa. What is Emma’s precise kinship term to Carl, using only standard English blood‑ and in‑law relations?
explanation: Emma is the daughter of Tom (John’s maternal uncle) and Lisa. Carl is Peter’s brother (John’s paternal uncle). Emma and Carl share no blood link; the only connection is through Lisa’s sister Nina, who is Carl’s spouse. Standard kinship terms do not cover this affinal chain, so no direct term exists.
choices: B) B) First cousin once removed
D) D) No standard direct relation (affinal chain only)

question: M and N are full siblings. M marries P; N marries Q. P’s sibling is R, and Q’s sibling is S. R and S marry each other and have a child T. What is the precise kinship term for the relation between T and M’s child?
explanation: P and R are siblings, so their children (M’s child and T) are children of siblings. Hence they share a common set of grandparents and are first cousins. No other shared ancestry exists.

question: Let X and Y be two persons. X’s mother is the sister of Y’s father, and Y’s mother is the sister of X’s father. Assuming no other intermarriages, what is the most precise standard kinship term for the relation between X and Y?
explanation: X’s maternal aunt is Y’s father, making Y’s paternal grandparents X’s maternal grandparents. Similarly, X’s paternal aunt is Y’s mother, so X’s paternal grandparents are Y’s maternal grandparents. Thus X and Y share both pairs of grandparents, i.e., they are double first cousins—the only term that captures this doubled ancestry.

question: In a family with no adoption and monogamous marriages, K’s mother has exactly one brother. That brother has exactly one daughter, who in turn has exactly one child L. What is the precise kinship term for L’s relation to K using standard English kinship terminology?
explanation: K’s mother’s brother is K’s maternal uncle. His daughter is K’s first cousin. L is the child of that cousin, making L a first cousin once removed of K. No other blood link exists, so the term is uniquely determined.

question: N’s only paternal uncle (the sole brother of N’s father) is married to N’s only maternal aunt (the sole sister of N’s mother). They have a child M. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation of M to N?
explanation: M is the child of N’s paternal uncle and maternal aunt, who are themselves a married couple. Thus M shares both sets of grandparents with N, making M a double first cousin—the most specific term.

question: In a family, X is the child of the brother of Y's mother, and Y is the child of the sister of X's father. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is the precise relationship between X and Y?
explanation: X is the child of Y's maternal uncle, making X Y's first cousin on the maternal side. Likewise, Y is the child of X's paternal aunt, making Y X's first cousin on the paternal side. In both cases the relation is first cousins; no further information guarantees a double‑cousin status.

question: John is married to Mary. He says, "My father's sister is also Mary's mother." Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed, remarriage permitted), what is the precise relation of John to Mary's mother?
explanation: John's father's sister is his paternal aunt. The statement makes this aunt Mary's mother, so Mary's mother is John's aunt. Therefore John is the nephew of Mary's mother.

question: M is the mother of N. N's father is O. O's sister is P. P's son is Q. Q's daughter is R, whose mother is S. S's brother is T, and T's child is U. Using standard English kinship terms (in‑law limited to spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, and children’s spouses), what is U's relation to M?
explanation: M → O (spouse) → P (sibling‑in‑law) → Q (nephew‑in‑law) → S (spouse) → T (sibling‑in‑law) → U (nephew/niece‑in‑law). The chain extends beyond the immediate in‑law scope and introduces no blood link, so no standard direct kin term exists.
choices: A) No standard direct relation (affinal chain only)

question: A’s mother is B. B’s brother is C. C’s daughter is D. D’s son is E. Using standard English kinship terms (blood only), what is the precise relation of E to A?
explanation: B’s brother C is A’s maternal uncle. C’s daughter D is A’s first cousin. D’s son E is the child of that cousin, making E A’s first cousin once removed (downward). No other term is more exact.

question: Y’s mother has exactly one brother, and Y’s father has exactly one brother. Those two brothers are married to each other and have a single child X. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed, remarriage permitted), what is the most precise relationship of X to Y?
explanation: X is the child of Y’s maternal uncle and also the child of Y’s paternal uncle. Because those uncles are spouses, X shares both sets of grandparents with Y, making X Y’s double first cousin – the only term that captures the doubled ancestry.

question: X's mother has exactly one brother, and X's father has exactly one sister. The brother of X's mother is married to the sister of X's father, and they have a child Y. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the precise relation between X and Y?
explanation: Y is the child of X's maternal uncle (mother's brother) and paternal aunt (father's sister). Thus Y is X's first cousin on both the maternal and paternal sides, sharing both grandparent pairs. The exact term is double first cousin.

question: N’s father has a sister (A) and N’s mother has a brother (B). A and B are married and have a child M. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy), what is the most precise relation between M and N?
explanation: A is N’s paternal aunt, B is N’s maternal uncle. Their child M is simultaneously the child of N’s paternal aunt and maternal uncle, making M a double first cousin of N.

question: M is N's mother. N's father O has a sister P, whose son is Q. Q's daughter is R, whose brother S marries T. T is the only child of the brother of M's father. What is T's relation to N?
explanation: M and T are first cousins (children of siblings). N is M's child, so N is one generation below M. Therefore N is the first cousin once removed of T, making T also the first cousin once removed of N.

question: Brothers A and B each marry sisters C and D, respectively. A and C have a son X; B and D have a daughter Y. No other marriages occur. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise description of the relationship between X and Y?
explanation: X and Y share both sets of grandparents: A’s parents are also B’s parents’ brothers‑in‑law, and C’s parents are also D’s parents. Thus they are first cousins through both paternal and maternal lines, i.e., double first cousins—the only term that captures the doubled ancestry.

question: In Family X, brother P and sister Q are siblings. In Family Y, brother R and sister S are siblings. P marries S and they have a child U. Q marries R and they have a child V. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation between U and V?
explanation: U and V share both sets of grandparents because each parent pair is a cross‑marriage of the two sibling pairs. Hence they are not merely first cousins; they are double first cousins, the exact term for this doubled ancestry.

question: M and N are siblings. Their aunt Q has two children, P and R, who are siblings. M marries P and N marries R. Each couple has one child: X (child of M & P) and Y (child of N & R). Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation between X and Y?
explanation: M and N share the same parents, and P and R share the same parents (Q’s). Moreover, M is a first cousin of P, and N is a first cousin of R. Hence X and Y share both sets of grandparents, making them double first cousins – the only term that captures the double shared ancestry.

question: In Family X, brother P and sister Q are siblings. In Family Y, brother R and sister S are siblings. P marries S and has a child A; Q marries R and has a child B. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is the most precise relation between A and B?
explanation: A and B are children of two couples who are each composed of a brother from one family and a sister from the other. Hence A and B share both sets of grandparents, making them double first cousins—the only term that captures this doubled ancestry.

question: X’s mother has exactly one brother, and X’s father has exactly one brother. The child of the mother’s brother is Y; the child of the father’s brother is Z. If either Y or Z is called W, what is W’s relation to X using standard English kinship terms?
explanation: Both Y and Z are children of X’s parents’ brothers. A child of a parent’s sibling is, by definition, a first cousin. The relation is uniquely determined and no other term fits.

question: M and N are siblings. M’s only child, O, marries P, who is the only child of N’s only sibling (a half‑brother Q). If O and P have a child R, what is the most precise standard English kinship term for R to Q?
explanation: Q is a half‑uncle of O (half‑brother of O’s mother/father). P is Q’s niece/nephew (child of Q’s half‑sibling). R is therefore both the grandchild of Q’s half‑sibling and the great‑niece/nephew of Q. The relationship cannot be uniquely expressed by a single standard term; it is ambiguous between great‑niece/nephew and half‑first cousin once removed.
choices: B) B) Half‑first cousin once removed

question: Alice is the mother of Bob. Carol is the sister of Alice’s husband. Dave is Carol’s son. Eve is Bob’s daughter. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed, remarriage permitted), what is Dave to Eve?
explanation: Bob is the child of Alice’s husband, Frank. Carol, Frank’s sister, makes Dave Frank’s nephew, hence Bob’s first cousin. Eve, as Bob’s daughter, is one generation below Bob, so Dave is a first cousin once removed to Eve.
choices: B) B) First cousin once removed
D) D) No standard direct relation

question: M has a sister N. N is married to O. O's sister P has a son Q. Q's mother is R, who is the daughter of M's brother S. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is the relation of M to Q?
explanation: S is M's brother, so R (S's daughter) is M's niece. Q is R's son, making Q the child of M's niece. The parent of a niece/nephew is a great‑uncle or great‑aunt. Since M is male, the precise term is great‑uncle.
choices: A) A) First cousin once removed
D) D) No standard kinship term

question: L’s mother is the sister of O’s father, and L’s father is the brother of O’s mother. Using only standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is the most precise term for the relationship between L and O?
explanation: Through L’s mother and O’s father, L is O’s first cousin. Through L’s father and O’s mother, L is also O’s first cousin. Because both of L’s parents are siblings of O’s parents, L and O share both sets of grandparents, making them double first cousins—the most specific label.

question: In a family with no adoption or remarriage, let P be the child of the only brother of Q’s mother, and let Q be the child of the only brother of P’s mother. Using standard English kinship terms only, what is the precise relationship between P and Q?
explanation: P is the child of Q’s maternal uncle, and Q is the child of P’s maternal uncle. The two uncles are different men (otherwise the mothers would be sisters, creating half‑siblings). Thus P and Q are each other’s child of a parent’s sibling – the definition of first cousins. No other qualifier applies.

question: John had two children with different wives: Adam and Beth. Adam married Clara, who is Diana’s daughter. Beth married Diana. Adam and Clara have a daughter Emma. Beth and Diana have a son Frank. Using standard English blood‑kinship terms only, what is Emma’s precise relation to Frank?
explanation: Diana is mother of Clara and also Beth’s spouse, so Clara and Frank share Diana as a common parent and are half‑siblings. Emma is Clara’s child, making her the child of Frank’s half‑sibling. Therefore Emma is Frank’s half‑niece (or half‑nephew).

question: M and N are brother and sister. M marries X and N marries Y. X and Y are also brother and sister. M and X have a child P; N and Y have a child Q. Using standard English kinship terms and without ignoring the double ancestry, what is the most precise relation between P and Q?
explanation: P and Q share both sets of grandparents because their parents are two pairs of siblings who married each other. This makes them first cousins on both sides, i.e., double first cousins, the exact term required.

question: John’s mother has a brother who is married to a woman. That woman is also the sister of John’s half‑sibling (the child of John’s father and his former spouse). What is the precise standard English kinship term for that woman in relation to John?
explanation: The woman is the wife of John’s maternal uncle, making her John’s aunt by marriage. No blood link exists, and standard kinship treats an uncle’s wife simply as an aunt. Hence the precise term is “aunt”.

question: M is the child of the sister of N’s father, and also the child of the brother of N’s mother. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the precise relation of M to N?
explanation: M is the child of N’s paternal aunt (father’s sister) and also the child of N’s maternal uncle (mother’s brother). Both describe the same relationship, making M N’s cousin on both sides – a double first cousin.

question: In a family with no adoption or other intermarriages, let R be a person. R’s mother has a brother (maternal uncle) and R’s father has a sister (paternal aunt). The uncle and aunt are married and have a child X. What is the most precise standard kinship term for X to R?
explanation: X is the child of R’s maternal uncle (mother’s brother) and paternal aunt (father’s sister). Thus X shares both of R’s grandparents on the mother’s side and on the father’s side, making X a double first cousin of R.

question: M’s mother has exactly one brother, who is the father of L. M’s father has exactly one brother, who is the father of K. If we select either L or K and call that person S, what is S’s precise relation to M using standard English kinship terms?
explanation: L is the child of M’s maternal uncle; K is the child of M’s paternal uncle. In either case S is the child of a parent’s brother, which is the definition of a first cousin. No other relationship fits.

question: A and B are siblings. A has a son C. B is married to D. D's sister is E, and E is the mother of F. Using only standard English kinship terms (in‑law limited to spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, children’s spouses), what is the relation of F to C?
explanation: C is A's son; A and B share parents. B’s spouse D is unrelated by blood to C. E is D’s sister, so E is only connected to C through two marriage links. F is E’s child, giving only an affinal chain with no blood link. Standard kin terms do not cover such a chain, so no direct term exists.
choices: A) No standard direct relation (affinal chain only)

question: M and P are a married couple. They have two children, N and O (full siblings). M’s brother and P’s sister are a married couple; they have two children, Q and R (full siblings). N marries Q and they have a child S. O marries R and they have a child T. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation between S and T?
explanation: N and O share both parents; Q and R share both parents. Their children S and T therefore share both sets of grandparents, giving them the exact status of double first cousins.

question: Y's mother has a sister S1, and Y's father has a brother B1. S1 and B1 marry each other and have a child X. No other intermarriages exist. Using standard English blood‑relation terms (no in‑law designations), what is the most precise relation of X to Y?
explanation: X is the child of Y's maternal aunt (S1) and paternal uncle (B1). Because those two spouses are themselves siblings of Y's parents, X shares both of Y's grandparent pairs. Hence X and Y are double first cousins, the exact term for this doubled shared ancestry.

question: L has one sister and one brother. The sister’s only son is X, and X’s child is M. The brother’s only daughter is Y, and Y’s child is N. What is the precise kinship term for the relation between M and N using standard English kinship terminology?
explanation: X (nephew) and Y (niece) are children of L’s siblings, so they are first cousins. Their children, M and N, are therefore children of first cousins, which makes M and N second cousins. No half‑ or removed relationships are involved.
choices: B) B) First cousins once removed

question: N’s mother has exactly one brother, and N’s father has exactly one sister. The brother and the sister each have a child, and those two children are the same person, M. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is M’s precise relation to N?
explanation: M is the child of N’s maternal uncle (first cousin) and also the child of N’s paternal aunt (first cousin). Sharing both pairs of grandparents makes M a double first cousin of N – the most specific term.

question: M’s mother has a brother U, whose daughter is V. M’s father has a sister W, whose son is T. V and T marry and have a child C. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy), what is the precise relation of C to M?
explanation: U is M’s maternal uncle, so V is M’s first cousin. W is M’s paternal aunt, so T is also M’s first cousin. V and T are therefore double first cousins. Their child C is one generation down, making C a double second cousin of M. The term “double second cousin” uniquely captures the doubled ancestry.

question: M is the only child of A. A has a sister B, whose son is C. C’s daughter D marries M’s son E. Using only standard English blood‑kinship terms (ignore any in‑law terminology), what is D’s precise relationship to A?
explanation: B is A’s sister, so C is A’s nephew. D, being C’s daughter, is A’s grand‑niece (the child of a nephew). The marriage to E introduces an affinal link, but the question restricts to blood relations only; thus the correct term is grand‑niece.

question: Two brothers, Adam and Brian, each marry two sisters, Clara and Diana, respectively. Adam and Clara have a child, Ethan; Brian and Diana have a child, Fiona. Assuming no other relationships, what is the most precise standard English kinship term for the relationship between Ethan and Fiona?
explanation: Ethan and Fiona share both sets of grandparents: Adam and Brian share the same parents, and Clara and Diana share the same parents. Thus they have two common grandparent pairs, making them double first cousins—the most exact term.

question: Anna and Ben are half‑siblings: they share the same mother but have different fathers. Anna has a son Carl, and Ben has a daughter Dana. Assuming no other intermarriages, what is the precise kinship term for the relationship between Carl and Dana?
explanation: Carl and Dana are children of half‑siblings, so they share only one grandparent (the common mother). The exact term for their relation is half‑first cousins.

question: John is married to Mary. Mary's sister Linda is married to Tom. Tom's brother Paul is the father of Sarah. Sarah is married to Mike, who is John's brother. What is Sarah's relation to Mary using standard English kinship terms?
explanation: Mary and Sarah are linked only via a marriage chain: Mary’s sister married Tom; Tom’s brother Paul is Sarah’s father. There is no blood connection and no direct in‑law relationship, so English kinship provides no standard term.
choices: C) No standard direct relation (affinal chain only)

question: In a family: M and N are siblings. M has a daughter O. N has a son P. O marries Q, who is the child of P’s sister R. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed, remarriage permitted), what is the precise relation between O and Q?
explanation: R is N’s daughter, so R is O’s first cousin. Q is R’s child, making Q O’s first cousin once removed. Because O is also Q’s spouse, the blood relation remains first cousin once removed.
choices: A) A) First cousin once removed
D) D) No blood relation (in‑law only)

question: M’s mother has a brother named N. N has a daughter O, and O has a son P. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the precise relation of P to M?
explanation: N is M’s maternal uncle, so O is M’s first cousin. P, being O’s son, is one generation down from that cousin, making him M’s first cousin once removed. No other listed term applies.
choices: B) B) First cousin once removed

question: T is the child of the sister of U's father, and also the child of the sister of U's mother. Using standard English kinship terms only, what is the precise relation of T to U?
explanation: U's paternal aunt (father's sister) and maternal aunt (mother's sister) are each a sibling of a parent. T, being the child of either aunt, is the child of a parent's sibling, which is a first cousin. The two aunts are distinct, so no doubling occurs.
choices: D) D) No standard direct relation

question: Two brothers, M and N, each marry a sister, A and B respectively. M + A have a child C; N + B have a child D. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy, but remarriage allowed), what is the most precise relation between C and D?
explanation: C and D share both paternal grandparents (M and N’s parents) and both maternal grandparents (A and B’s parents). Sharing a full set of grandparents twice makes them double first cousins, a distinct term from ordinary first cousins.

question: J has a father and a mother. J’s father has a sister who has exactly one child; that child is P. J’s mother has a brother who has exactly one child; that child is Q. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy, remarriage allowed), what is the precise relation of each of P and Q to J?
explanation: J’s father’s sister is J’s paternal aunt; her only child P is J’s first cousin. Similarly, J’s mother’s brother is J’s maternal uncle; his only child Q is also J’s first cousin. Both share a grandparent pair and are therefore first cousins.

question: Two brothers marry two sisters (no other intermarriages). The first brother’s child is X; the second brother’s child is Y. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation between X and Y?
explanation: X and Y share both sets of grandparents because their fathers are brothers and their mothers are sisters. This makes them first cousins with doubled ancestry, i.e., double first cousins—the most exact term.

question: In a monogamous family with no adoption, let L be a person. M is the child of the only brother of L’s mother. What is the precise kinship term for M’s relation to L?
explanation: The only brother of L’s mother is L’s maternal uncle. The child of that uncle is L’s first cousin. No other blood link is involved, so the exact term is “first cousin.”
choices: C) C) First cousin once removed

question: A man has two wives. With his first wife he fathers a son S, and with his second wife he fathers a daughter D. D marries a man H. H has a sister W, who marries S. S and W have a child C. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption), what is the precise relation of C to D?
explanation: S and D are half‑siblings (share a father). The child of a half‑sibling is a half‑niece/nephew. The marriage of S to W (H’s sister) does not change the blood link; C is still the child of D’s half‑brother, so C is D’s half‑niece/nephew.
choices: D) D) No standard direct relation

question: M’s father has a sister who has a daughter N. M’s mother has a brother who has a son P. Assuming no intermarriage between the two families, what is the most precise standard kinship term for the relation between N and P?
explanation: N is M’s paternal first cousin (child of his father’s sister). P is M’s maternal first cousin (child of his mother’s brother). Their lineages trace back to different sets of grandparents, so they share no common ancestor. Hence there is no consanguineous relation; the correct term is simply “no blood relation.”

question: M’s mother is the sister of N’s father. M is married to O, who is the child of P. P is the sibling of Q, and Q is the parent of N. Using standard English kinship terms (ignoring in‑law extensions), what is the precise blood relation of M to N?
explanation: M’s mother and N’s father are siblings, so M and N share the same set of grandparents. That makes them first cousins, regardless of the extra marital connections described.

question: P’s father has a sister S, and P’s mother has a brother B. S and B marry each other and have a child M. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed, remarriage permitted), what is the precise relation between M and P?
explanation: M is the child of P’s paternal aunt (father’s sister) and maternal uncle (mother’s brother). Thus M shares both sets of grandparents with P, making them double first cousins – the most specific term.

question: John is married to Emma. John’s sister Mary has a son Peter. Peter marries Linda. Linda’s mother Susan is Emma’s sister. Peter and Linda have a child Alex. Using standard English kinship terms (blood relations only, in‑law terms limited to spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, children’s spouses), what is Alex’s relation to John?
explanation: Peter is John’s nephew (son of John’s sister). Alex is Peter’s child, so Alex is John’s grandnephew, i.e., John is Alex’s granduncle (great‑uncle). The marriage of Linda adds no blood link, so the precise term is granduncle/great‑uncle.

question: M’s mother is the sister of N’s father, and M’s father is the brother of N’s mother. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relationship between M and N?
explanation: Each of M’s parents is a sibling of one of N’s parents, so M and N share both sets of grandparents. That makes them double first cousins – the exact term for cousins who share both grandparent pairs.

question: In a family with no adoption, monogamy allowed, remarriage permitted: Let P be the grandchild of the only brother of R’s mother. Let Q be the grandchild of the only sister of R’s father. If we select either P or Q and call that person S, what is S’s relation to R?
explanation: The brother of R’s mother and the sister of R’s father are R’s maternal uncle and paternal aunt. Their grandchildren are children of R’s first cousins, making them R’s first cousins once removed. Both possibilities give the same relation.

question: M and N are brother and sister. P and Q are another brother‑sister pair. M marries P and N marries Q. Their respective children are A (child of M & P) and B (child of N & Q). Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation between A and B?
explanation: A and B share both sets of grandparents because each pair of parents are siblings. They are therefore double first cousins – a more exact term than simple first cousins, half‑first cousins, or second cousins.

question: M and N share exactly one parent (they are half‑siblings). M has a child A; N has a child B. There are no other intermarriages. What is the precise standard English kinship term for A and B?
explanation: A and B are children of half‑siblings, so they share only one grandparent. The exact term for such relatives is "half‑first cousins".

question: X’s mother is the sister of Y’s father, and there are no other intermarriages in the families. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy), what is the precise relation of X to Y?
explanation: X’s mother and Y’s father are siblings, so they share the same parents. X is the child of Y’s father’s sister, making X the child of Y’s paternal aunt/uncle. The child of a parent’s sibling is a first cousin. Hence X and Y are first cousins.

question: Two brothers, Adam and Ben, each marry a woman; Adam marries Clara and Ben marries Diana. Clara and Diana are sisters. Adam and Clara have a child X; Ben and Diana have a child Y. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy), what is the most precise relationship between X and Y?
explanation: X’s father Adam and Y’s father Ben are brothers, and X’s mother Clara and Y’s mother Diana are sisters. Thus X and Y share both sets of grandparents, making them double first cousins—the only term that captures the doubled ancestry.

question: John is the son of Mary's brother. Mary's sister is the mother of Paul's father. Paul is married to Linda, who is the daughter of John's mother. What is Paul to John in standard English kinship terms?
explanation: Mary, her brother, and her sister are siblings. John is nephew of Mary and also nephew of Mary's sister, making Mary's sister John's aunt. She is Paul's paternal grandmother, so Paul's father is child of John's aunt – John's cousin. Paul, being the child of that cousin, is John's first cousin once removed. The marriage to Linda (John's sister) does not change the blood link.

question: X's mother has a brother U, whose daughter is Y. X's father has a sister V, whose son is Z. Y and Z marry and have a child W. What is the precise kinship term for W's relation to X, using standard English kinship terms?
explanation: Y is X's maternal first cousin and Z is X's paternal first cousin. W is the child of each of those first cousins. The child of a first cousin is a first cousin once removed, so W is X's first cousin once removed.

question: L’s mother has exactly one brother, and L’s father has exactly one brother. Each brother has exactly one child, and those two children are the same person M. Using standard English kinship terms, what is M’s relation to L?
explanation: M is the child of L’s maternal uncle and also the child of L’s paternal uncle, sharing both pairs of grandparents. This makes M and L double first cousins, the precise term.

question: John’s mother has a brother named Tom. Tom is married to Lisa, who is the sister of John’s wife Mary. Using only standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation of Tom to John?
explanation: Tom is the brother of John’s mother, making him John’s maternal uncle. Although Tom is also John’s brother‑in‑law through the marriage of his sister‑in‑law Lisa, the primary blood relation dictates the standard term “uncle.”

question: John is the son of Mary and Paul. Mary’s brother is Tom. Tom’s daughter is Lisa. Lisa’s son is Mark. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is Mark’s relation to John?
explanation: Tom is Mary’s brother, so he is John’s maternal uncle. Lisa, Tom’s daughter, is John’s first cousin. Mark, Lisa’s son, is one generation below John’s cousin, making John and Mark first cousins once removed.

question: M’s mother has a brother U, and M’s father has a sister V. U and V marry each other and have a child W. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy, remarriage allowed), what is the exact relation of W to M?
explanation: U is M’s maternal uncle and V is M’s paternal aunt. Their child W shares both sets of grandparents with M, giving the precise term double first cousin.

question: F and H are siblings. E is the only child of F. G is the only child of H. I is the child of G. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the relation of E to I?
explanation: F and H being siblings makes their children E and G first cousins. I is G's child, one generation below G. Therefore E is one generation above I’s parent, giving them the precise term “first cousin once removed.”

question: M and N are brother and sister. M marries X and N marries Y, where X and Y are also brother and sister. M and X have a child A; N and Y have a child B. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation between A and B?
explanation: A and B share both of their paternal grandparents (M and N’s parents) and both of their maternal grandparents (X and Y’s parents). Sharing both grandparent pairs makes them double first cousins, a stricter term than ordinary first cousins.

question: L has exactly one sister and exactly one brother, each married to unrelated partners. The only son of L's sister has a child X. The only daughter of L's brother has a child Y. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the precise blood relation between X and Y?
explanation: L's sister's son and L's brother's daughter are children of two siblings (L's sister and brother), so they are first cousins. X and Y are the children of those first cousins, making X and Y second cousins.

question: M is the mother of N and O. O’s sister T is also M’s child. N is married to P. P’s sister Q is married to no one. R is the father of S, and S’s mother is T. Using standard English kinship terms (in‑law limited to spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, children’s spouses), what is Q’s relation to S?
explanation: T and N are siblings, so N is S’s aunt/uncle. Q is P’s sister, i.e., N’s sister‑in‑law. To S, Q is therefore an aunt‑in‑law. No closer blood term exists.

question: M is the child of the only sibling of L’s father, and also the child of the only sibling of L’s mother (the two siblings are different people). Using standard English kinship terms, what is M’s relation to L?
explanation: M is the child of L’s paternal uncle and also of L’s maternal uncle. Therefore M shares both sets of grandparents with L, making them double first cousins—the precise term.

question: In a family with no adoptions, L’s mother has exactly one brother, and L’s father has exactly one sister. P is the child of that brother, and also the child of that sister (the two spouses are unrelated). What is P’s precise relationship to L?
explanation: P is the child of L’s maternal uncle and also the child of L’s paternal aunt. In either case P is the child of a parent’s sibling, which by standard kinship is a first cousin. The double‑parent link does not change the basic degree of cousinship.

question: In a family with no adoption, monogamy (remarriage allowed), let Z be the only brother of L’s mother and also the only brother of L’s father (the two brothers are different men). If X is the child of Z, what is X’s precise relation to L using standard English kinship terms?
explanation: Z is L’s maternal uncle and also L’s paternal uncle. X, as Z’s child, is simultaneously the child of L’s maternal uncle and the child of L’s paternal uncle, sharing both pairs of grandparents. This makes X a double first cousin of L.

question: Two brothers, Alan and Brian, each marry two sisters, Clara and Diana, respectively. Alan and Clara have a child, X. Brian and Diana have a child, Y. Assuming no other intermarriages, what is the most precise standard English kinship term for the relation between X and Y?
explanation: X and Y share both sets of grandparents because their fathers are brothers and their mothers are sisters. This double sharing makes them double first cousins, a more specific term than ordinary first cousins.

question: L's father has exactly one sibling, a sister named A. L's mother has exactly one sibling, a brother named B. A and B are married and have a single child C. Assuming no adoption or polygamy, what is the most precise standard kinship term for C relative to L?
explanation: C is the child of L's paternal aunt (A) and maternal uncle (B). Thus C shares both sets of grandparents with L, making them first cousins on both sides—i.e., double first cousins. No other term is more exact.

question: M and N share only their mother (they are half‑siblings). M has one child, X; N has one child, Y. No other marriages or adoptions occur. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relationship between X and Y?
explanation: X and Y are children of half‑siblings, so they share exactly one grandparent. The correct term is “half‑first cousins,” which denotes sharing a single grandparent rather than the full pair required for plain first cousins.

question: John and Mary are half‑siblings (they share only their mother). John’s only child is Alice; Mary’s only child is Bob. Alice and Bob each marry unrelated partners and have one child each, Carol and Dave respectively. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation between Carol and Dave?
explanation: John and Mary share one parent, so Alice and Bob are half‑first cousins (they share a single grandparent). Their children, Carol and Dave, therefore share one great‑grandparent, making them half‑second cousins. No other shared ancestors exist, so the precise term is “half‑second cousins.”

question: John married Anna first, then Beth (no children together). Anna had a son Carl from a previous marriage; Beth had a daughter Diana from a previous marriage. Carl and Diana marry and have a child Emma. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption), what is Emma’s precise relation to John?
explanation: Carl is John’s stepson and Diana is his stepdaughter. Their child Emma is therefore John’s step‑grandchild. No blood link exists, so “step‑grandchild” is the most specific standard term.
choices: D) D) No standard direct kinship term

question: M’s mother first married X and had a daughter L. After X’s death she married Y and had M. Y had a son N from a previous marriage. L and N marry and have a child Z. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy but remarriage allowed), what is Z’s precise relation to M?
explanation: L is M’s half‑sister (same mother). N is M’s half‑brother (same father). Z, their child, is therefore the child of both a half‑sister and a half‑brother of M. In standard kinship the child of a sibling (half or full) is called a niece or nephew; the double line does not change the term. Hence Z is M’s niece/nephew.

question: Alice and Ben are half‑siblings (they share only a mother). Alice has a daughter Carla and Ben has a son David. No other marriages connect the families. What is the precise kinship term between Carla and David?
explanation: Carla and David are each the child of half‑siblings Alice and Ben, who share only one parent. Hence Carla and David share exactly one grandparent. Children of half‑siblings are called “half‑first cousins”. Full first cousins need both grandparents; second cousins share great‑grandparents.

question: In a family, X is the child of a man A and a woman B. Y is the child of a man C and a woman D. A and D are brothers, and B and C are sisters. No other marriages link these families. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation between X and Y?
explanation: X and Y share both sets of grandparents: A and D share the same father, and B and C share the same mother. Thus they have two common grandparent pairs, which makes them double first cousins – the precise term for this situation.

question: John and Mary are siblings. John marries Alice, and Mary marries Bob. Alice and Bob are also siblings. John and Alice have a daughter Clara; Mary and Bob have a son David. Using standard English kinship terms (no in‑law extensions), what is the most precise relation between Clara and David?
explanation: Clara and David share both sets of grandparents: John‑Mary’s parents and Alice‑Bob’s parents. Hence they are first cousins through two independent lines, i.e., double first cousins, which is more specific than plain first cousins.

question: M and N are siblings. O and P are siblings. M marries O and has a child X; N marries P and has a child Y. Assuming no other intermarriages, what is the most precise standard English kinship term for the relation between X and Y?
explanation: M and N are siblings; O and P are siblings. X is child of M and O; Y is child of N and P. X and Y share both sets of grandparents (parents of M/N and parents of O/P), so they are double first cousins. No other term is more precise.

question: John and his brother Tom share both parents. John’s sister Mary has a son (John’s nephew). Tom has a daughter (John’s niece). The nephew marries the niece and they have a child. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is the precise relation of that child to John?
explanation: The child is the offspring of John’s nephew (his sister’s son) and John’s niece (his brother’s daughter). That makes the child John’s great‑nephew if male or great‑niece if female. Because gender is not specified, the exact term cannot be uniquely determined.

question: I have a child, M, who is described as the child of the only son of my father's sister and also the child of the only daughter of my mother's brother. Using standard English kinship terms, what is M's relation to me?
explanation: The two described parents could be the same individual (if my paternal aunt’s son and my maternal uncle’s daughter are the same person), making M my sibling, or they could be distinct individuals, making M my double first cousin. Since the information does not specify, the precise kinship cannot be fixed.

question: L's mother has exactly one brother, and L's father has exactly one sister. The child of that brother and the child of that sister are the same person, M. What is M's precise relationship to L using standard English kinship terms?
explanation: M is the child of L's maternal uncle and also the child of L's paternal aunt. Thus M shares both sets of grandparents with L, making M a double first cousin—the most specific term for this dual‑lineage first‑cousin relationship.

question: John’s mother Mary has a brother Tom. John’s father Alan has a sister Susan. Tom is married to Susan, and they have a daughter Lily. John has a daughter Emma. Using standard English kinship terms (in‑law limited to spouse), what is Emma’s precise relation to Lily?
explanation: Tom is John’s maternal uncle and Susan is John’s paternal aunt; their daughter Lily is John’s double first cousin. Emma, as John’s child, is the child of Lily’s double first cousin, making Emma Lily’s first cousin once removed.

question: M is the mother of J. J is married to L. L’s brother is K. K’s daughter is N. P is the son of M’s brother’s wife (i.e., the child of M’s brother and his spouse). P is married to N. What is the most precise standard English kinship term for the relation between N and J?
explanation: M’s brother’s child P is J’s first cousin. N is P’s spouse, so N is J’s cousin‑in‑law. No blood term applies, and “cousin‑in‑law” is the recognized affinal label.
choices: C) C) No standard direct relation

question: M’s mother has exactly one brother, whose only child is A. M’s father has exactly one sister, whose only child is B. A and B marry each other and have a child C. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy, remarriage allowed), what is C’s relation to M?
explanation: A is M’s maternal first cousin (child of mother’s brother). B is M’s paternal first cousin (child of father’s sister). Their child C is thus the child of M’s first cousin on both sides, making C M’s first cousin once removed. The relationship is uniquely determined.

question: Brothers A and B each marry sisters C and D respectively; A and C have a son X, B and D have a son Y. X and Y each have a child, P and Q respectively. Using standard English kinship terms without ignoring doubled ancestry, what is the most precise relation between P and Q?
explanation: X and Y are double first cousins (they share both sets of grandparents). Their children P and Q therefore share both sets of great‑grandparents, making them double second cousins – the precise term.
choices: C) C) First cousins once removed

question: L has one brother and one sister. The brother has only a daughter, who in turn has a child M. The sister has only a son, whose own child also has a child M (i.e., M is the grandchild of that son). Using standard English kinship terms, what is M’s precise relation to L?
explanation: Both lines trace back to L’s parents, who are M’s great‑grandparents. L is a child of those parents; M is a great‑grandchild. Sharing a grandparent makes first cousins; the two‑generation gap adds “twice removed.” Hence M is L’s first cousin twice removed.
choices: B) B) First cousin twice removed

question: Two brothers, M1 and M2, marry two sisters, F1 and F2. M1 and F1 have a son S1. M2 and F2 have a daughter D1. S1 and D1 marry and have a child C. What is the most precise standard kinship term for C’s relation to M1?
explanation: C is the child of M1’s son, so C is M1’s grandson. D1 is M1’s niece (daughter of his brother M2), so C is also M1’s grandnephew. The precise description is that C is both grandson and grandnephew.
choices: C) Both grandson and grandnephew (double relation)

question: Person A’s father and Person B’s mother are siblings, and Person A’s mother and Person B’s father are also siblings. No other intermarriages occur. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation between Person A and Person B?
explanation: Each of A’s parents is a sibling of one of B’s parents, so A and B share both sets of grandparents. That makes them double first cousins, a more specific term than plain first cousins.

question: In a monogamous family tree with no adoptions: M and N are siblings. M has a daughter A. N has a son B. A and B marry each other and have a child C. What is the most precise standard English kinship term for C’s relationship to M’s mother?
explanation: M’s mother is also N’s mother, making her C’s great‑grandmother on the paternal side and grandmother on the maternal side. The closest single term is “great‑aunt”, because C is the child of the grandchild (A) of that woman’s other child (N). No standard term captures both lines, so “great‑aunt” is the precise label.
choices: D) D) No standard direct relation

question: L has one brother and one sister. The brother has exactly one daughter, who in turn has a child M. The sister has exactly one son, who in turn has a child N. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the precise relation between M and N?
explanation: L’s brother’s daughter and L’s sister’s son are children of two siblings, so they are first cousins. M and N are each the child of those first cousins; children of first cousins are second cousins. No half‑blood or other complication exists, making "second cousins" the exact term.

question: In a family, siblings M and N each have two children. M’s children are A and D; N’s children are B and E. A marries B, and D marries E. A and B have a child C; D and E have a child F. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is the most precise relationship between C and F?
explanation: C and F share both pairs of grandparents, since each pair of their parents are first cousins who themselves are children of the same two siblings. Therefore C and F are double first cousins, the most precise term.

question: John and Mary are siblings. Mary marries Tom, who is the brother of John’s wife Anna. John and Anna have a son Sam. Tom and Mary have a daughter Lily. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relationship between Sam and Lily?
explanation: Sam is child of John (Mary’s brother) and Anna (Tom’s sister). Lily is child of Mary (John’s sister) and Tom (Anna’s brother). Thus Sam and Lily are children of two pairs of siblings, sharing both sets of grandparents – they are double first cousins.

question: M and N are siblings. M marries P and N marries Q. P and Q are also siblings. M and P have a child X; N and Q have a child Y. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relationship between X and Y?
explanation: X and Y are children of two sibling pairs. They share both sets of grandparents (M/N’s parents and P/Q’s parents). Hence they are first cousins through both parental lines, i.e., double first cousins – the most precise term.

question: Anna and Beth are sisters. Carl and Dave are brothers. Anna marries Carl and they have a child Emma. Beth marries Dave and they have a child Frank. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy), what is the most precise relation between Emma and Frank?
explanation: Emma and Frank share both sets of grandparents because their mothers are sisters and their fathers are brothers. Hence they are first cousins on the maternal side and also first cousins on the paternal side, making them double first cousins, the exact term.

question: A man named Aaron has two children: a son Brian and a daughter Clara. Clara has a daughter Diana. Brian marries Diana. Using standard English kinship terms (including spouse), what is the most precise description of Diana’s relation to Brian?
explanation: Diana is Brian’s niece by blood (daughter of his sister) and also his wife by marriage. No single standard term captures both aspects simultaneously, so the relation is not uniquely determinable.

question: Two sisters, A and B, marry two brothers, C and D, respectively. A and C have a son X; B and D have a son Y. X and Y each marry unrelated partners and have children P and Q. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation between P and Q?
explanation: A and B are sisters; C and D are brothers. Their children X and Y share both sets of grandparents, making them double first cousins. Consequently, P and Q share both sets of great‑grandparents, which is precisely called double second cousins.

question: M’s mother has a brother whose daughter is N. M’s father has a sister whose son is O. N and O marry and have a child C. Using standard English kinship terms (no in‑law extensions), what is C’s relation to M?
explanation: N is M’s maternal first cousin; O is M’s paternal first cousin. Their child C is one generation below each cousin, making C a first cousin once removed to M on both sides. No closer term applies.
choices: B) B) First cousin once removed
D) D) No direct kinship term

question: M is the child of the only sibling of N’s father, and also the child of the only sibling of N’s mother. Assuming no intermarriage among the siblings, what is the most precise kinship term for M’s relation to N?
explanation: M is the child of N’s paternal uncle and also the child of N’s maternal aunt. Thus M shares both sets of grandparents with N, making them double first cousins—the only term that captures the doubled ancestry.

question: M is the only child of his father's second wife. N is the child of M's mother's brother. Using standard English kinship terms, what is N's relation to M?
explanation: M's mother is his father's second wife. Her brother is M's maternal uncle. The child of an uncle is a first cousin. Therefore N is M's first cousin.
choices: D) D) No blood relation (affinal only)

question: L has exactly one sister S and exactly one brother B. S has exactly one child C, and B has exactly one child D. C and D marry each other and have a single child M. Using standard English kinship terms (blood relations only), what is M's relation to L?
explanation: C is L's niece and D is L's nephew. Their child M is therefore the child of a niece/nephew, which makes M L's grandniece (if female) or grandnephew (if male). Both parental lines give the same term, so the precise relation is grandniece/grandnephew.

question: John is the son of Mary. Mary has a sister Linda. Linda’s son Paul has a daughter Emma. Using standard English blood‑kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is the precise relation of John to Emma?
explanation: Mary and Linda are sisters, so Linda is John’s aunt. Paul, Linda’s son, is John’s first cousin. Emma, Paul’s daughter, is one generation below Paul, making her John’s first cousin once removed. No closer term applies.

question: R’s mother has exactly one brother. That brother is married to the only sister of R’s father. What is the precise kinship term for the child of this couple in relation to R, using standard English kinship terminology?
explanation: The couple consists of R’s maternal uncle and paternal aunt. Their child is the offspring of both a maternal uncle and a paternal aunt, sharing both sets of grandparents with R. Hence the child is a double first cousin of R.

question: In a family with no adoption and monogamous marriages between unrelated persons: M’s father’s sister, Anna, has a son Ben. Ben has a daughter Clara. Using standard English kinship terms, what is Clara’s precise relation to M?
explanation: Anna is M’s paternal aunt, so Ben is M’s first cousin. Clara, being Ben’s daughter, is one generation below a first cousin, making her M’s first cousin once removed.

question: L's mother has exactly one brother, A, and L's father has exactly one brother, B. A marries C and B marries D, where C and D are sisters. A and C have a child X; B and D have a child Y. Assuming no other intermarriages, what is the most precise standard English kinship term for the relation between X and Y?
explanation: X and Y share both sets of grandparents because their fathers are brothers of L's parents and their mothers are sisters. This makes them double first cousins, a term distinct from ordinary first cousins.

question: L’s mother has exactly one brother, and L’s father has exactly one sister. The child of that brother and the child of that sister are the same person M. What is the precise kinship term for M’s relation to L, using standard English kinship terminology?
explanation: M is the child of L’s maternal uncle and also of L’s paternal aunt. Since those two spouses are each a sibling of one of L’s parents, M shares both sets of grandparents with L, making M a double first cousin—the most specific standard term.

question: R's father has exactly one brother, U, whose daughter is V. R's mother has exactly one sister, W, whose son is X. V and X marry and have a child Y. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is Y's precise relationship to R?
explanation: V is R's paternal first cousin; X is R's maternal first cousin. Y is the child of each of those first cousins, making Y a first cousin once removed of R on both sides. No closer or double‑cousin term applies.
choices: C) C) First cousin once removed
D) D) No standard relation (affinal only)

question: Two brothers, Adam and Brian, each marry two sisters, Clara and Diana respectively. Adam and Clara have a son Ethan. Brian and Diana have a daughter Fiona. Assuming no other marriages, what is the most precise kinship term for Ethan and Fiona?
explanation: Adam and Brian share both parents, and Clara and Diana share both parents. Their children therefore share both paternal and maternal grandparents. The exact term for such children is double first cousins.

question: M and N are siblings. M marries O, whose brother is P. P marries Q, who is the daughter of N. R is the child of M and O, and S is the child of P and Q. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed, remarriage permitted), what is the precise relation between R and S?
explanation: R’s parents are M (sibling of N) and O (sibling of P). S’s parents are P (sibling of O) and Q (child of N). Thus R and S each have the same two sets of grandparents, just swapped. Sharing both grandparent pairs makes them double first cousins, the most specific term.

question: John is the father of Mary. Mary's brother Tom is married to Susan, who is the daughter of John's sister Linda. Mary has a son Peter. What is Peter's relation to Susan using standard English kinship terms (in‑law limited to spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, and children’s spouses)?
explanation: Tom is Mary's brother, so Susan (Tom's wife) is Mary's sister‑in‑law. Peter is Mary's son, making Susan his aunt by marriage, i.e., aunt‑in‑law. No blood term applies.

question: M’s mother has one sister, Anna. M’s father has one brother, Ben. Anna is married to Ben, and they have a child, Lily. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is Lily’s precise relation to M?
explanation: Lily is the child of M’s maternal aunt (Anna) and paternal uncle (Ben). A child of a sibling of one’s mother or father is a first cousin. She shares one grandparent from each side, so the correct term is first cousin.

question: Maya and Nina are sisters. Omar and Paul are brothers. Maya marries Omar and they have a son Sam. Nina marries Paul and they have a son Lee. Sam and Lee are double first cousins. Sam marries an unrelated woman and has a daughter Ava; Lee also marries an unrelated woman and has a daughter Zoe. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relationship between Ava and Zoe?
explanation: Sam and Lee share both paternal and maternal grandparents, making them double first cousins. Their children each inherit both sets of great‑grandparents, so Ava and Zoe share both pairs of great‑grandparents. The correct term for such a pair is double second cousins.

question: In a monogamous family with no adoption, A and B are married. A's brother C marries B's sister D, and they have a child E. Using standard English kinship terms (blood only, with in‑law limited to spouse and spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, children’s spouses), what is E to A?

question: L has one sister and one brother. The sister has exactly one son, and the brother has exactly one daughter. Their respective children are the same person, M. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy, remarriage allowed), what is the precise relation of M to L?
explanation: M is the child of L's sister’s son (L’s nephew) and also the child of L's brother’s daughter (L’s niece). In both cases M is the child of a niece or nephew, which is called a grandniece or grandnephew (great‑niece/nephew). Hence D is correct.

question: M and N are siblings. M has a daughter O. N has a son P. P’s child is Q. What is the precise blood relationship between O and Q (ignoring their marriage, if any)?
explanation: M and N share both parents, so O and P are first cousins. Q is P’s child, making Q one generation below P. Hence O is one generation above Q, and they are first cousins once removed. No other shared ancestors change this classification.

question: M and N are siblings. P and Q are siblings. M marries Q, and N marries P. Their children, A (child of M & Q) and B (child of N & P), meet. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation between A and B?
explanation: A and B each have the same two fathers’ parents and the same two mothers’ parents, because their parents are two married sibling pairs. Sharing both sets of grandparents makes them double first cousins, the exact term.

question: L’s mother has exactly one son, and L’s father has exactly one daughter. The son of L’s mother (her brother) marries the daughter of L’s father (his sister), and they have a child M. question: In a family, M and N are siblings. M has a daughter O. N has a son P. O and P marry each other and have a child Q. Ignoring adoption and assuming monogamy, what is the most precise standard English kinship term for Q’s relation to M’s brother?

question: N is a person. P is the child of the only brother of N’s mother, and also the child of the only brother of N’s father. Assuming monogamy, no adoption, and that the two brothers are different individuals, what is the precise standard kinship term for P relative to N?
explanation: P is the child of N’s maternal uncle (mother’s brother) and also the child of N’s paternal uncle (father’s brother). Each makes P a first cousin of N. Since the two uncles are unrelated, there is no doubling; the exact term is simply “first cousin.”

question: In a monogamous family with no adoption, let X be the child of the only brother of Y’s mother and also the child of the only sister of Y’s father. Who is X to Y?
explanation: X’s mother is Y’s paternal aunt and X’s father is Y’s maternal uncle (they are married). Thus X is the child of both a sibling of Y’s father and a sibling of Y’s mother, making X a double first cousin of Y – they share all four grandparents. No other term fits.

question: I have exactly one maternal uncle and exactly one paternal uncle, and each of them has exactly one child. If I pick either of those children, what is that person's precise relationship to me using standard English kinship terms?
explanation: Both the child of my mother's brother and the child of my father's brother are children of a parent’s sibling. That makes each child a first cousin, regardless of which side they come from. No other relationship fits.

question: In a family with no adoption, monogamy allowed but remarriage permitted: my mother’s brother married my father’s sister, and they have a child X. What is the exact kinship term for X to me?
explanation: X is the child of my maternal uncle and my paternal aunt, thus sharing both of my grandparents. The precise term for such a relative is a double first cousin.

question: Alice’s mother has a brother named Ben. Ben’s daughter is Clara, and Clara has a son named David. Using standard English kinship terms, what is David’s precise relation to Alice?
explanation: Ben is Alice’s maternal uncle, making Clara her first cousin. Clara’s son David is one generation younger than Clara, so he is Alice’s first cousin once removed. This is the only exact term that fits.

question: John and Mary are married. John’s sister Lisa is married to Peter. Peter’s brother Tom is married to Mary’s brother Kevin. What is Tom’s relation to Lisa using standard English kinship terms (in‑law limited to spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, children’s spouses)?

question: Mary has a brother. That brother’s son is John. What is the precise standard English kinship term for John’s relation to Mary?

question: M is the mother of N and O. N is married to P. P's sister Q is married to R, who is O's son. What is the precise kinship term for Q with respect to N, using standard English kinship vocabulary?
explanation: O is N's sibling, so O's son R is N's nephew. Q is the spouse of that nephew, making Q N's niece‑in‑law. No blood link exists, and the spouse‑of‑nephew relation has a unique standard term.

question: M and N are married. M’s only sibling is the parent of P, and N’s only sibling is also the parent of P. Assuming no incest and monogamy, what is the precise kinship term for P relative to the child Q of M and N?
explanation: P is the child of M’s sibling (maternal aunt/uncle) and also the child of N’s sibling (paternal aunt/uncle). Thus P and Q share both sets of grandparents, making them double first cousins – the most specific standard term.

question: Adam and Brian are full brothers. Adam has a daughter Clara. Brian has a son David, who in turn has a son Ethan. Before any marriage, what is the precise kinship term for the relation between Clara and Ethan?
explanation: Adam and Brian share both parents, so Clara (Adam’s child) and David (Brian’s child) are first cousins. Ethan is David’s son, making Ethan one generation below David. Therefore Ethan is Clara’s first cousin once removed. No other shared ancestry changes this classification.

question: M and N are siblings. M marries O, who is the only child of P. N marries Q, who is the only child of R. O and Q are first cousins. If X is the child of M and O, and Y is the child of N and Q, what is the most precise standard English kinship term for the relation between X and Y?

question: Tom’s mother has a brother Alan, whose daughter is Beth. Tom’s father has a sister Carol, whose son is Dave. Beth and Dave marry and have a child Emma. What is Emma’s precise relationship to Tom, using standard English kinship terms?
explanation: Beth is Tom’s maternal first cousin; Dave is Tom’s paternal first cousin. Emma is the child of Tom’s first cousin (both sides), making her Tom’s first cousin once removed. No other standard term fits more precisely.

question: A's mother has exactly one brother, B. B has exactly one child, C. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is the precise relationship between A and C?
explanation: B is A's maternal uncle (mother's brother). His child C is therefore A's first cousin. No other blood links exist, making "first cousin" the exact term.

question: M and N are brothers. X and Y are sisters. M marries X and N marries Y. No other intermarriages occur. M and X have a child A; N and Y have a child B. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relationship between A and B?
explanation: A and B share both sets of grandparents (M‑N’s parents and X‑Y’s parents). Hence they are first cousins through two independent sibling links, i.e., double first cousins – the only term that captures the doubled ancestry.

question: A and B are two children. A's father is the brother of B's mother, and A's mother is the sister of B's father. No other intermarriages exist. What is the most precise standard English kinship term for the relationship between A and B?
explanation: A and B share both sets of grandparents because each of their parents are siblings of the other's opposite parent. Hence they are first cousins on both sides, i.e., double first cousins, which is the most specific term.

question: Alice and Bob are siblings. Alice has a son Charlie. Bob has a daughter Dana. Charlie and Dana marry and have a child Eve. What is Eve's precise relation to Alice, using standard English kinship terms?

question: Let Y be a person. Y’s mother has exactly one brother, and Y’s father has exactly one sister. Those two siblings (the maternal uncle and the paternal aunt) are married and have a child X. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation of X to Y?

question: Let M be a person. Let A be the only child of M’s mother, and let B be the only child of M’s father. If P is the child of A and Q is the child of B, what is the precise kinship term for P in relation to Q?
explanation: M’s mother’s only child is M, and M’s father’s only child is also M, so A = B = M. Both P and Q are children of M, making them siblings (brother or sister). No other relationship applies.

question: M and N are full siblings. M has two children, A (with spouse X) and D (with spouse Y). N has one child, B (with spouse Z). A and B marry and have a child C. D has a child E. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the precise relation between C and E?

question: John and Mary are half‑siblings, sharing only their mother. John has a son Peter, and Mary has a daughter Susan. No other marriages or adoptions exist. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the precise relation between Peter and Susan?
explanation: Peter and Susan are children of half‑siblings, so they share exactly one grandparent (the common mother’s parent). The correct term for such a relationship is "half‑first cousins"; full first cousins require both grandparents in common.

question: L’s father has a sister named Anna, and L’s mother has a brother named Ben. Anna and Ben marry each other and have a child M. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy), what is the most precise relation of M to L?
explanation: M is the child of L’s paternal aunt (father’s sister) and maternal uncle (mother’s brother). Thus M shares both sets of grandparents with L, making M a double first cousin—the exact term for this doubled ancestry.

question: M’s mother has a brother who is married to a woman named L. L’s sister is the sister of M’s father. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the relation of L’s sister to M?
explanation: M’s mother’s brother is M’s maternal uncle. His wife L is the aunt‑by‑marriage. L’s sister is identified as the sister of M’s father, i.e., the paternal aunt. Therefore L’s sister is M’s aunt (paternal).

question: P is the only child of the only brother of Q’s mother, and also the only child of the only sister of Q’s father. Assuming no adoption, what is the most precise standard kinship term for P’s relation to Q?

question: Maya has a brother Leo and a sister Nina. Leo has a son Carl, and Nina has a daughter Dana. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation between Carl and Dana?

question: Mary has a son John. Mary's brother Peter is married to Linda. Linda's sister Susan has a son Tom. Using standard English kinship terms (excluding step‑ and in‑law beyond spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, and children's spouses), what is Tom to John?

question: M and N are siblings. M has two children, A and D; N has two children, B and E. A marries B and they have a child C. D marries E and they have a child F. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the precise relation between C and F?

question: Emma and Liam share the same mother but have different fathers. Emma’s only child is Noah, and Liam’s only child is Ava. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy allowed), what is the most precise relationship between Noah and Ava?

question: A's mother and B's father are siblings, and A's father and B's mother are also siblings. No other intermarriages occur. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the precise relation between A and B?
explanation: A shares both sets of grandparents with B because each of A's parents is a sibling of one of B's parents. Thus they are double first cousins.

question: In a family where N’s father has exactly one sister and N’s mother has exactly one brother, M is the child of that sister and also the child of that brother. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy), what is the precise relation of M to N?
explanation: M is the child of N’s paternal aunt (father’s sister) and also the child of N’s maternal uncle (mother’s brother). Both lines make M a first cousin of N, and because the relationship occurs through two independent sibling links, M is a double first cousin of N.

question: Two brothers, John and Mark, marry two sisters, Emma and Lucy respectively. John and Emma have a son Paul. Mark and Lucy have a daughter Mary. Paul and Mary marry and have a child Sam. question: A's mother has exactly one brother, and A's father has exactly one sister. The maternal uncle and paternal aunt are married to each other and have a single child B. Using standard English kinship terms (no adoption, monogamy), what is B's precise relation to A?
explanation: B is the child of A's maternal uncle (mother's brother) and paternal aunt (father's sister). Thus B shares both sets of grandparents with A, making them double first cousins—the most specific term for this doubled relationship.

question: In a monogamous, non‑adoptive family tree, X’s mother is the sister of Y’s father, and X’s father is the brother of Y’s mother. Y’s parents are unrelated to each other. What is the most precise standard kinship term for the relation between X and Y?

question: Adam and Ben are brothers. Adam’s wife Clara has a sister Diana. Ben marries Diana. Adam and Clara have a daughter Eva; Ben and Diana have a son Frank. Using standard English kinship terms, what is the most precise relation between Eva and Frank?

question: In a family with no adoption and monogamous marriages, X is the son of the brother of Y’s mother. Using standard English kinship terms, what is X’s relation to Y?

question: X’s mother’s brother’s son and X’s father’s sister’s daughter marry each other. What is the precise standard English kinship term for X’s relation to the child of that couple?

question: M’s mother is the sister of N’s father. M is married to O, whose brother is P. P’s wife is Q, and Q is the daughter of N. Using standard English kinship terms (blood only, with spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, children’s spouses), what is Q’s relation to M?

question: Two brothers, A and B, each marry two sisters, C and D, respectively. A and C have a son X; B and D have a son Y. X and Y marry unrelated partners and each have a child (P and Q).
